title: The Pump Handle That Stopped an Epidemic
creator: Footnotes with Priya
description:
In 1854 a doctor took the handle off a water pump in Soho, and changed how we think about disease forever. Or did he? The real story is messier.

This episode is brought to you by the Blue Thread Foundation, which builds and maintains clean water points in rural communities. Learn more or give at bluethread.org/footnotes

Sources:
Snow, J. On the Mode of Communication of Cholera (1855)
Johnson, S. The Ghost Map (2006)

Patreon: patreon.com/footnoteswithpriya

sentences.t: In the summer of 1854, people in one small corner of London started dying, fast.
Within three days, more than a hundred and twenty people on a handful of streets were dead.
And the disease was cholera, which, if you don't know it, is genuinely one of the most horrifying ways to go.
You can go from healthy at breakfast to dead by dinner, just from losing water.
Now at the time, almost every respectable doctor in London had the same explanation.
Bad air, miasma, the idea that disease floated up out of rotting stuff as a kind of poisonous smell.
And honestly, if you'd walked through Soho in 1854, you'd have believed it too.
There were cesspits under houses, there was no proper sewer system, and it smelled, constantly.
But there was one doctor, John Snow, who thought the smell was a distraction.
He thought cholera was in the water.
And what he did next is the part everyone remembers, so let's get the myth out of the way first.
The story usually goes, Snow drew a map, saw the deaths cluster around one pump on Broad Street, took the handle off, and the epidemic stopped.
And that's, sort of, true, but it skips the interesting bits.
Before we get into what actually happened on Broad Street, I want to tell you about something that connects pretty directly to this story.
This episode is brought to you by the Blue Thread Foundation.
They're a nonprofit that builds and repairs clean water points in rural communities, wells, filters, rainwater systems, the whole thing.
And here's what I like about them, they don't just drill a well and leave.
They train local technicians and pay them to keep the pumps running, because a broken pump is basically no pump.
Around two billion people still drink water that isn't safely managed, and cholera is still out there because of it.
If you want to help, you can give once or monthly at bluethread.org slash footnotes, that link's in the description.
Even a small monthly gift helps cover a technician's wages, and they publish where every project is on a live map.
Thanks to the Blue Thread Foundation for supporting the channel.
Okay, so, Broad Street.
Snow didn't actually start with the map, he started by knocking on doors.
He went house to house asking one question, where do you get your water?
And a pattern jumped out almost immediately, the dead families had mostly drunk from the Broad Street pump.
But the really convincing evidence was the exceptions.
There was a brewery right near the pump, and none of the brewery workers got sick.
Why, because they were given free beer every day and basically never drank the water.
I love that, I love that the control group in this story is a bunch of guys drinking beer at work.
And then there was a widow who lived miles away, in Hampstead, who died of cholera that same week.
Nobody near her was sick, so how did she get it?
It turned out she used to live in Soho, she liked the taste of the Broad Street water, and she had a bottle of it delivered to her every day.
Which is, I mean, it's tragic, but as evidence it's almost perfect.
So Snow takes all this to the local board, and they agree, a bit reluctantly, to take the handle off the pump.
And here's the part the myth leaves out, the epidemic was already slowing down by then.
A lot of people had fled the area, and the outbreak may have already peaked.
Snow himself admitted it was hard to say how much the handle actually did.
And after the panic passed, the board put the handle back, and mostly went back to believing in bad air.
It took years, and another big outbreak, for the water theory to really win.
So Snow didn't stop an epidemic with a wrench, not exactly.
What he did was something slower and more important, he showed you could find a cause by counting carefully.
That's basically the birth of epidemiology, a guy with a notebook, walking door to door.
Next time, we're going to look at the Great Stink of 1858, when the Thames smelled so bad Parliament finally had to do something.
Thanks for watching, and I'll see you in the footnotes.
